metadata.file_name: Brit J Math   Statis - 2025 - Tang - A path signature perspective of process data feature extraction.pdf
metadata.title: A path signature perspective of process data feature extraction
metadata.venue: British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The empirical case study uses PIAAC 2012 Cycle I PSTRE process data from 17 countries, restricted to participants who completed all 14 PSTRE items and to 13 of the 14 items due to an incomplete codebook for item U21. The manuscript does not report the use of PIAAC sampling weights or replicate weights, and it does not name any weight variables (e.g., TOTWGT or replicate-weight schemes). The predictive comparisons are implemented via generalized linear models with L1 feature selection and L2 regularization, evaluated using five-fold cross-validation; these procedures are described without any explicit complex-survey weighting. Given the absence of stated weight application, the analysis should be treated as unweighted with respect to population representativeness, and results should be interpreted as evidence about predictive utility of process features rather than population-level causal effects.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study’s dependent variables in the empirical case study are background variables (age, gender, ICTHOME) and process-based score quality metrics (correlations, Kendall’s tau, MSE) rather than PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes. Because the paper does not describe any PV generation/combination procedure and does not report a missing-data strategy for the analytic sample beyond excluding participants with missing values for each target variable, the missing-data handling is not fully documented. This is a reporting gap for transparency, especially because the paper relies on cross-validation and feature selection steps that can be sensitive to how missingness is handled.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PIAAC 2012 Cycle I PSTRE process data from 17 countries. The analytic dataset includes response processes for 12,108 participants who completed all 14 PSTRE items. Due to an incomplete codebook for item U21, response processes from 13 out of 14 items are used. System events automatically generated by the computer to summarize interface state changes are removed as redundant. For each predicted background variable (age, gender, ICTHOME), participants with missing values on that target variable are removed from the analysis.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 Cycle I PSTRE process data (13 items; 17 countries)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Five-fold cross-validation OSR2 (exact numeric values not tabulated; Figure 12 shows Models 1/2 outperform baseline and TLS(5) improves OSR2).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 Cycle I PSTRE process data (13 items; 17 countries), the study leveraged polytomous PSTRE scores and time-sequence-derived TLS(5) process features (with L1-selected log-signature features) to predict age, finding that timestamp-sequence features improve out-of-sample prediction over baseline item scores and that TLS features capture the information contained in simpler time summaries. This indicates that more granular timing information in adult problem-solving processes can improve measurement of respondent characteristics, suggesting that assessment systems should incorporate richer process-time features rather than relying only on final item scores.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 Cycle I PSTRE process data (13 items; 17 countries)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Five-fold cross-validation prediction accuracy (exact numeric values not tabulated; Figure 12 shows ALS(20,2) improves prediction over baseline; time-only models do not substantially improve).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 Cycle I PSTRE process data (13 items; 17 countries), the study leveraged action-sequence-derived ALS(20,2) log-signature features (with L1-selected features) together with baseline polytomous PSTRE scores to predict gender, finding that action features substantially improve prediction while timestamp-sequence features add little incremental value. This indicates that gender differences in PSTRE performance are more strongly reflected in action patterns than in timing patterns, suggesting that process-based analytics for fairness/DIF diagnostics should prioritize action-sequence features for gender-related heterogeneity.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 Cycle I PSTRE process data (13 items; 17 countries)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Five-fold cross-validation OSR2 (exact numeric values not tabulated; Figure 12 shows Models using ALS(20,2) or TLS(5) outperform baseline and that combining ALS(20,2)+TLS(5) yields only small additional improvement).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 Cycle I PSTRE process data (13 items; 17 countries), the study leveraged action-sequence-derived ALS(20,2) and time-sequence-derived TLS(5) log-signature features (plus baseline polytomous PSTRE scores) to predict ICTHOME, finding that both action and timing features provide substantial predictive information but that their combination yields only a small incremental gain. This indicates that ICT familiarity is reflected in both how respondents act and how quickly they proceed, implying that process-based scoring and DIF mitigation efforts should consider both action and time features while recognizing substantial overlap in the information they capture.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 Cycle I PSTRE process data (13 items; 17 countries; repeated 50 times)
main_findings.target_variable: Process-based PSTRE score quality vs IRT-based score (Pearson correlation, Kendall’s tau, MSE)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pearson’s correlation, Kendall’s tau, and MSE between process-based scores and reference IRT-based scores (Figure 15 shows process-based scores outperform IRT-based; exact numeric values not tabulated).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 Cycle I PSTRE process data (13 items; 17 countries; repeated 50 times), the study leveraged TLS(5), ALS(20,2), and combined PLS(20,2) log-signature features to construct process-based PSTRE scores and compared them to IRT-based scores, finding that all process-based scores outperform the IRT-based reference on correlation and error metrics, with PLS(20,2)+TLS(5) (process features) performing best. This indicates that incorporating both action and time information can improve the precision of latent trait assessment from interactive problem-solving tasks, supporting policy and practice moves toward process-informed scoring models in large-scale adult assessments.

data.outcome_summary: This paper proposes a path-signature-based feature extraction method that jointly represents action sequences and response-time sequences from computer-based interactive problem-solving items. In the empirical case study, the authors analyze PIAAC 2012 Cycle I PSTRE process data from 17 countries, using 12,108 participants who completed all 14 PSTRE items, with item U21 excluded due to an incomplete codebook and system-generated interface events removed. They evaluate predictive utility using generalized linear models with L1 feature selection and L2 regularization, assessed via five-fold cross-validation (OSR2 for continuous targets and prediction accuracy for gender). Results show that time-sequence log-signature features (TLS(5)) improve age and ICTHOME prediction beyond polytomous item scores, while action-sequence features (ALS(20,2)) are more informative for gender. Finally, process-based PSTRE scores derived from log-signature features outperform IRT-based scores on Pearson correlation, Kendall’s tau, and MSE, suggesting improved precision from richer process-time representations; however, the manuscript does not report a complete missing-data strategy and does not document survey-weight usage.
